body:
OBJECTIVES
- Students know the relative sizes of units within one system (km, m, cm; kg, g; lb, oz; L, mL; hr, min, sec) and express larger units in terms of smaller ones, recording equivalents in a two-column table (4.MD.A.1).
- Students use the four operations to solve word problems involving distances, time, liquid volume, masses and money (4.MD.A.2).
- Students apply the area and perimeter formulas for rectangles in real-world problems, including finding an unknown side (4.MD.A.3).
- Students make a line plot of measurements in fractions of a unit (1/2, 1/4, 1/8) and solve addition and subtraction problems using it (4.MD.B.4).

MATERIALS
- Rulers marked in eighths of an inch, meter sticks and yardsticks
- A balance or kitchen scale with gram masses; a liter bottle and a measuring cup in milliliters
- Grid paper for drawing rectangles
- Ten real bean sprouts (or paper strips cut to the lengths in the activity) for measuring

FIVE-DAY PLAN
Day 1: Read Measure, Convert and Plot. Measure the classroom door in feet and in inches and compare. Lesson: Measurement Units and Conversions; build conversion tables together.
Day 2: Area and perimeter mini-lesson on grid paper: draw a 9 by 6 rectangle, count the square units, then use the formulas. Start Garden Plans.
Day 3: Finish Garden Plans, including the money and time problems. Use a number line to show elapsed time.
Day 4: Measure sprouts (or paper strips) to the nearest eighth of an inch and build a class line plot. Assignment: Line Plots: Bean Sprout Lengths.
Day 5: Assessment: Measurement and Data Check.

DIFFERENTIATION
- Support: keep conversion tables posted; use grid paper for every area and perimeter problem so students can count to check.
- Support: for elapsed time, provide an open number line with hour and minute jumps.
- Stretch: find all the rectangles with whole-number sides and an area of 36 square feet, and the perimeter of each.
- Multilingual learners: pair each unit with a real object (a gram is about a paper clip, a kilogram is about a textbook, a liter is a large water bottle). Many students already use metric units at home; invite them to share.

FAMILY NOTE (send home at the start of the unit)
We are measuring this unit: lengths, masses, liquid volume and time. Your child is learning that 1 foot is 12 inches, 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams, and 1 hour is 60 minutes, and how to find the area and perimeter of rectangles. At home, ask your child to measure a table or a rug and find its perimeter, or to work out how long until dinner. Cooking with measuring cups is great practice too.
title: Teacher guide: Measurement and Data
